Chapter Six: Healing Emotional Wounds—Integrating Inner Restoration with Deliverance.
Now that we’ve laid the groundwork for deliverance and daily spiritual upkeep, let’s take a look at the next step—healing those emotional wounds that can quietly fuel spiritual struggles.
Here’s something to consider: real spiritual freedom and emotional healing are deeply connected. You rarely get one without the other. Wounds like rejection, betrayal, or abandonment? They don’t just sting—they can actually draw in negativity, making it tough to stay free unless you intentionally choose to heal.
Think about it like caring for a real injury. If you cut your hand, you have to clean it, protect it, and give it time to heal. If you ignore it, it might get infected—turning into resentment, bitterness, or a habit of always putting up walls. Emotional wounds work the same way. They need gentle, ongoing attention.
So, how do you actually start healing? The book lays out a few gentle, practical steps.
First, you’ve got to acknowledge the pain. This means being honest about what hurts, without brushing it off or making excuses. Maybe you write it down, talk to someone you trust, or take it to prayer—whatever helps you really see and name what’s going on inside.
Next, it’s about inviting divine healing right into those broken places. This isn’t just sitting back and hoping for the best—it’s an active step. You ask for comfort, for a new perspective, even for restoration. You’re working together with something bigger, reaching for wholeness.
Another key step? Replacing lies with truth. Emotional wounds often come bundled with false beliefs—thoughts like, “I’m unlovable,” “I’ll always be alone,” or “It’s all my fault.” Spotting these lies and intentionally speaking truth over them is a game changer for deep healing.
And, don’t forget self-compassion. Just like you’d care for a hurting friend, the book encourages you to treat yourself with that same kindness and patience as you heal.
Let’s make this real with an example. Picture someone who’s carried the weight of rejection for years. That wound has shaped how they see themselves and how they connect with others. But when they finally name the pain, invite spiritual comfort, and start replacing the old story of “I’m not worthy” with the truth that they have real value, something shifts. Suddenly, new freedom shows up in their relationships and their sense of self.
Remember, emotional healing isn’t a one-and-done thing. It’s a journey. Some wounds close up quickly, but others take more time and care, almost like peeling away layers of an onion. Every layer brings fresh insight and a bit more release. The key? Stay patient. Be persistent. Trust that with each step, you’re moving closer to true wholeness.
